nodes.label: Civil War
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Violent conflict between opposing groups within a country that becomes so intense it resembles a war. Sri Lanka's ethnic conflict between Sinhalas and Tamils is an example. Often results from failure to share power and accommodate diversity.

nodes.label: John Stuart Mill
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: British philosopher and advocate of individual liberty. Wrote 'On Liberty' (1859). Formulated the harm principle: state can restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others. Champion of free speech and individual autonomy. Key thinker for UPSC political theory.

nodes.label: Harm Principle
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: J.S. Mill's principle that the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community against their will is to prevent harm to others. One's own good is not sufficient warrant. Foundation of liberal limits on state power.

nodes.label: Freedom of Expression
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Right to express opinions, ideas, and beliefs without censorship. Includes freedom of press. Essential for democracy. Can be restricted on grounds of defamation, incitement, public order, sovereignty. NCERT emphasizes this as cornerstone of democratic freedom.

nodes.label: Self-Regarding Actions
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Mill's concept: actions that affect only the person performing them and do not harm others. The state has no right to interfere with self-regarding actions. Wearing a seatbelt or helmet debates arise from this distinction.

nodes.label: Other-Regarding Actions
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Actions that affect others and may cause harm. According to Mill, the state can legitimately restrict only other-regarding actions. The difficulty lies in determining whether an action is truly self-regarding or affects others.

nodes.label: Natural Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: All humans are born equal in dignity and rights regardless of birth, caste, race, or gender. Basis of human rights declarations. Does not deny natural differences in abilities but asserts equal moral worth.

nodes.label: Positive Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights requiring the state to take positive action: provide education, healthcare, housing. Second-generation rights. In India, many are DPSPs rather than enforceable fundamental rights. Right to education became fundamental through 86th Amendment.

nodes.label: Group Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights held by groups rather than individuals: indigenous peoples, linguistic minorities, religious communities. Includes right to self-governance, cultural preservation. Tension with individual rights when group norms restrict individual freedom.

nodes.label: Soviet System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Socialist political and economic system established after the 1917 Russian Revolution. Centred on the Communist Party with no opposition allowed. Economy was planned and state-controlled. Ensured minimum living standards but became bureaucratic and authoritarian.

nodes.label: Evolution of Law in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In ancient India, overlapping local laws with unequal punishments based on caste. Colonial period: British claim of introducing rule of law is disputed - colonial law was arbitrary (Sedition Act 1870, Rowlatt Act). Indian nationalists fought for law as justice, not mere obedience.

nodes.label: Worker's Worth and Vulnerability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Due to massive unemployment, workers are easily replaceable and willing to work in unsafe conditions for wages. Employers exploit this vulnerability to ignore safety. The low compensation to Bhopal victims reflected the perceived low worth of Indian workers. Accidents regularly occur at construction sites, mines, and factories.
